TRADE ADJUSTMENT ASSISTANCE (TAA) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET AND HOW TAA DIFFERS FROM UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE AND WARN
This information sheet describes the federal Trade Adjustment Assistance (TAA) program for workers, authorized by the Trade Act of 1974 as amended, 19 U.S.C. § 2271 et seq. TAA is a separate federal program from the documents elsewhere in this corpus concerning California's state unemployment insurance (UI) system (the claimant information sheet, employer response, appeal, overpayment, and severance-and-UI documents, administered by California's Employment Development Department under the state Unemployment Insurance Code) and from the WARN Act documents (the federal and California WARN Acts, which require advance notice of certain layoffs and plant closings but do not themselves provide any wage-replacement, training, or relocation benefit). TAA instead is a federal program, administered by the U.S. Department of Labor, that can make extended income support (called Trade Readjustment Allowances, or TRA), job training, job search and relocation allowances, and a health coverage tax credit available to a group of workers whom the Department of Labor has certified as adversely affected by increased imports or a shift in production to a foreign country. Jordan Lee was employed by Acme, Inc. until March 2, 2026. This document states facts about how TAA eligibility is established and how TAA benefits relate to state unemployment insurance; it does not determine that Jordan Lee's own separation qualifies for TAA, and it is not itself a TAA petition or application.

CURRENT OPERATIONAL STATUS: TAA BENEFITS UNDER THIS PART ARE NOT CURRENTLY AUTHORIZED
The Trade Act of 1974's worker program, 19 U.S.C. §§ 2271-2298 (the sections describing petitions, certification, Trade Readjustment Allowances, training, and job search and relocation allowances), has lapsed. An editorial note carried in the current U.S. Code text following 19 U.S.C. § 2271 (and repeated after related sections in this part), captioned "Termination Date," states that no trade adjustment assistance, vouchers, allowances, or other payments or benefits may be provided under this part after June 30, 2022, except as otherwise provided. This is not a new or unusual event for this program: the same note and the amendment history recite a series of earlier lapses and temporary revivals (for example, a lapse addressed by a temporary revival running from 2011 to January 1, 2014, and a further temporary revival running from June 29, 2015 to July 1, 2021, after which the statute reverted to an earlier version before again lapsing on June 30, 2022). The text fetched for this document does not itself show a further reauthorization enacted after that June 30, 2022 lapse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  — 19 U.S.C. § 2271, Termination Date note (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 19 U.S.C. § 2271 note ("Termination Date") (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2271)

Having fetched and read the actual current 19 U.S.C. § 2271 text (and the parallel note on §§ 2272 and 2297) directly from Cornell's Legal Information Institute, the honest finding is that, as carried in that text, new TAA benefits under this part are not authorized after June 30, 2022, subject to whatever transition or savings provisions Congress may have separately enacted for petitions filed before that date (the "except as otherwise provided" language, and the detailed transition rules in note material accompanying Pub. L. 114-27 § 405, which this document does not attempt to restate in full). This document's drafter could not independently corroborate current program status against the Department of Labor's own TAA program pages, because the network access available for this research was blocked from reaching dol.gov; this finding rests on the Cornell-hosted U.S. Code text and its official notes alone, fetched twice with distinct User-Agent strings and confirmed byte-identical, without independent confirmation of whether Congress has since reauthorized the program in legislation not yet reflected in that text. A reader should not treat this document as confirming that any TAA benefit is currently obtainable for a new petition.

HOW A GROUP OF WORKERS BECOMES CERTIFIED: PETITION AND GROUP ELIGIBILITY
Under 19 U.S.C. § 2271(a)(1), an individual worker does not petition for TAA benefits alone. A petition for certification of eligibility to apply for adjustment assistance for a group of workers is instead filed simultaneously with the Secretary of Labor and with the Governor of the State where the workers' firm or subdivision is located, and may be filed by the group of workers itself, by the workers' certified or recognized union or other duly authorized representative, or by the workers' employer (acting together with one-stop operators or one-stop partners, on the workers' behalf). Once a petition is filed, 19 U.S.C. § 2272 sets out the group eligibility requirements the Secretary applies before certifying the group: the Secretary must determine that a significant number or proportion of the firm's workers have become, or are threatened to become, totally or partially separated, and that either (1) the firm's sales or production have decreased while imports of like or directly competitive articles increased and contributed importantly to the separations, or (2) the firm shifted production of such articles to a foreign country under the conditions § 2272(a)(2)(B) describes. Only after the Secretary certifies the group as eligible can members of that certified group individually apply for TAA benefits.

As the preceding clause discloses, new certifications and benefits under this part are not currently authorized past June 30, 2022 absent a further reauthorization this document's drafter could not independently confirm.

TRADE READJUSTMENT ALLOWANCES: HOW TRA FOLLOWS, RATHER THAN REPLACES, STATE UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
Trade Readjustment Allowances (TRA) are the extended income-support benefit available to a certified adversely affected worker. TRA does not replace state unemployment insurance and is not payable independently of it. Under 19 U.S.C. § 2291(a)(3), a worker qualifies for a TRA payment for a week of unemployment only if the worker was entitled (or would have been entitled) to unemployment insurance for a week within the applicable benefit period, has exhausted all rights to that unemployment insurance (except for state-funded additional compensation not reimbursed from federal funds), and has no unexpired waiting period remaining for it. In other words, a worker must first draw down, and exhaust, state UI eligibility before TRA becomes payable; TRA generally picks up where UI leaves off rather than running alongside it. The amount of TRA also derives directly from the worker's UI experience: under 19 U.S.C. § 2292(a), the weekly TRA amount equals the worker's most recent weekly UI benefit amount for a week of total unemployment preceding the worker's first exhaustion of UI, reduced (but not below zero) by any deductible training allowance and by income deductible from UI under the applicable state or federal disqualifying-income rules.

  — 19 U.S.C. § 2291(a)(3)(A) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 19 U.S.C. § 2291(a)(3)(A) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2291)

  — 19 U.S.C. § 2291(a)(3)(B)-(C) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 19 U.S.C. § 2291(a)(3)(B)-(C) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2291)

  — 19 U.S.C. § 2292(a) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 19 U.S.C. § 2292(a) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2292)
  Known gap: This corrects a framing choice in this document's research brief, which described the UI-TRA relationship only as TRA 'generally supplements/follows' UI without identifying the operative statutory mechanism. Having read the current text of §§ 2291(a)(3) and 2292(a) directly, the more precise statement is that UI exhaustion is an express eligibility condition for TRA, and the weekly TRA amount is computed from the worker's own prior UI weekly benefit amount rather than set independently. This clause does not cover the separate rule in § 2291(a)(4) tying TRA to the work-search and acceptance requirements of the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970, nor § 2292(b) and (c)'s separate rules for workers who are undergoing training or who receive a training allowance under other federal law, both of which can further affect the TRA amount or the count of weeks remaining. As the earlier clause in this document discloses, TRA payments under this part are not currently authorized for weeks after June 30, 2022, absent transition provisions or reauthorization not independently confirmed here.

TRAINING, JOB SEARCH ALLOWANCES, AND RELOCATION ALLOWANCES
Beyond TRA, the statute authorizes three other categories of benefit for a certified adversely affected worker. Training: under 19 U.S.C. § 2296(a), the Secretary of Labor may approve payment of training costs when the Secretary determines, among other conditions, that no suitable employment is available for the worker, the worker would benefit from appropriate training, there is a reasonable expectation of employment following training, and approved training is reasonably available. Job search allowances: under 19 U.S.C. § 2297, a worker who has been totally separated and cannot reasonably be expected to secure suitable employment in the local commuting area may apply for reimbursement of 90 percent of necessary job search expenses, up to a maximum of $1,250. Relocation allowances: under 19 U.S.C. § 2298, a worker who has obtained (or has a bona fide offer of) suitable long-term employment in another area, and cannot reasonably be expected to find suitable local employment, may apply for reimbursement of 90 percent of the reasonable and necessary expenses of moving the worker, the worker's family, and household effects, plus a lump-sum payment equal to three times the worker's average weekly wage, up to a maximum of $1,250.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  — 19 U.S.C. § 2296(a)(1) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 19 U.S.C. § 2296(a)(1) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2296)

  — 19 U.S.C. § 2297(b)(1)-(2) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 19 U.S.C. § 2297(b)(1)-(2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2297)

  — 19 U.S.C. § 2298(b)(1) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 19 U.S.C. § 2298(b)(1) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2298)
  "a lump sum equivalent to 3 times the worker’s average weekly wage, up to a maximum payment of $1,250."
  — 19 U.S.C. § 2298(b)(2) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 19 U.S.C. § 2298(b)(2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/19/2298)
  Known gap: This clause summarizes the qualifying conditions and dollar figures in 19 U.S.C. §§ 2296(a), 2297(a)-(b), and 2298(a)-(b) as currently printed; it does not cover the detailed application deadlines in §§ 2297(a)(2)(C) and 2298(a)(2)(E), the training-approval limitations and exceptions elsewhere in § 2296, or § 2298(c)'s further limitations on relocation allowances. It also does not independently verify whether these dollar caps have been adjusted by regulation since this text was last amended. As the program-status clause in this document discloses, none of these benefits are currently authorized for weeks or events after June 30, 2022, absent transition provisions or reauthorization not independently confirmed here.

THE HEALTH COVERAGE TAX CREDIT: A RELATED BENEFIT THAT EXPIRED EARLIER THAN THE REST OF TAA
Separately from the Trade Act benefits described above, the Internal Revenue Code has authorized a Health Coverage Tax Credit (HCTC) for certain individuals, including TAA recipients, at 26 U.S.C. § 35(a): a credit against federal income tax equal to 72.5 percent of the amount the taxpayer paid for qualified health insurance coverage for eligible coverage months. However, 26 U.S.C. § 35(b)(1)(A)(B) defines an "eligible coverage month" to include only a month that begins more than 90 days after the enactment of the Trade Act of 2002 and before January 1, 2022. On the face of this statutory text, the HCTC is therefore not available for coverage months beginning on or after January 1, 2022, regardless of the separate lapse of the other TAA benefits described above.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "there shall be allowed as a credit against the tax imposed by subtitle A an amount equal to 72.5 percent of the amount paid by the taxpayer for coverage of the taxpayer and qualifying family members under qualified health insurance for eligible coverage months beginning in the taxable year."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 35(a) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 26 U.S.C. § 35(a) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/35)
  "such month begins more than 90 days after the date of the enactment of the Trade Act of 2002, and before January 1, 2022."
  — 26 U.S.C. § 35(b)(1)(B) (U.S. Code, Cornell Legal Information Institute text), 26 U.S.C. § 35(b)(1)(B) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/35)
  Known gap: This is a second, independent correction to this document's research brief, which listed the health coverage tax credit as one of TAA's currently available benefits without qualification. Having fetched and read the current 26 U.S.C. § 35 text directly, the honest finding is that its own "eligible coverage month" definition ended before January 1, 2022 -- roughly six months earlier than the June 30, 2022 cutoff described for the other TAA benefits in the program-status clause above. This clause covers only § 35(a) and the relevant part of § 35(b)(1); it does not cover § 35's other eligibility conditions (qualifying-individual categories, the bar on other specified coverage, the incarceration exclusion, or the advance-payment mechanism), nor whether Congress has enacted a further extension not reflected in the fetched text. This document's drafter could not independently confirm current HCTC status against an IRS source; this finding rests on the Cornell-hosted U.S. Code text alone, fetched twice with distinct User-Agent strings and confirmed byte-identical.

GENERAL NATURE OF TAA BENEFITS, IN PLAIN TERMS
Taken together, the statutory provisions described in this document authorize four broad categories of benefit for a worker in a group the Department of Labor has certified as adversely affected by trade: (1) Trade Readjustment Allowances, which are weekly cash payments computed from the worker's own prior unemployment insurance benefit amount and payable only after the worker has exhausted regular unemployment insurance; (2) approved training, intended to help the worker qualify for suitable employment; (3) a job search allowance, reimbursing costs of looking for work outside the worker's local commuting area; (4) a relocation allowance, reimbursing moving costs and providing a lump-sum payment when a worker relocates for a new job; and, historically, (5) a health coverage tax credit toward the cost of health insurance premiums. This document does not state that Jordan Lee qualifies for any of these benefits, does not compute any amount Jordan Lee might receive, and is not a substitute for reviewing the current, effective text of 19 U.S.C. § 2271 et seq. and 26 U.S.C. § 35, including whatever transition or reauthorization provisions may apply after the termination date disclosed elsewhere in this document.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Jordan Lee acknowledges having received and reviewed this information sheet regarding the federal Trade Adjustment Assistance program, in connection with Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. that ended on March 2, 2026. This document is informational only. It does not itself constitute a TAA petition, application, or certification, and Jordan Lee understands that any such filing must be made directly with the U.S. Department of Labor and the applicable state agency.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause summarizes the qualifying conditions and dollar figures in 19 U.S.C. §§ 2296(a), 2297(a)-(b), and 2298(a)-(b) as currently printed; it does not cover the detailed application deadlines in §§ 2297(a)(2)(C) and 2298(a)(2)(E), the training-approval limitations and exceptions elsewhere in § 2296, or § 2298(c)'s further limitations on relocation allowances. It also does not independently verify whether these dollar caps have been adjusted by regulation since this text was last amended. As the program-status clause in this document discloses, none of these benefits are currently authorized for weeks or events after June 30, 2022, absent transition provisions or reauthorization not independently confirmed here.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the Trade Act benefits described above, the Internal Revenue Code has authorized a Health Coverage Tax Credit (HCTC) for certain individuals, including TAA recipients, at 26 U.S.C. § 35(a): a credit against federal income tax equal to 72.5 percent of the amount the taxpayer paid for qualified health insurance coverage for eligible coverage months. However, 26 U.S.C. § 35(b)(1)(A)(B) defines an "eligible coverage month" to include only a month that begins more than 90 days after the enactment of the Trade Act of 2002 and before January 1, 2022. On the face of this statutory text, the HCTC is therefore not available for coverage months beginning on or after January 1, 2022, regardless of the separate lapse of the other TAA benefits described above.

expectedJSON.gap: This is a second, independent correction to this document's research brief, which listed the health coverage tax credit as one of TAA's currently available benefits without qualification. Having fetched and read the current 26 U.S.C. § 35 text directly, the honest finding is that its own "eligible coverage month" definition ended before January 1, 2022 -- roughly six months earlier than the June 30, 2022 cutoff described for the other TAA benefits in the program-status clause above. This clause covers only § 35(a) and the relevant part of § 35(b)(1); it does not cover § 35's other eligibility conditions (qualifying-individual categories, the bar on other specified coverage, the incarceration exclusion, or the advance-payment mechanism), nor whether Congress has enacted a further extension not reflected in the fetched text. This document's drafter could not independently confirm current HCTC status against an IRS source; this finding rests on the Cornell-hosted U.S. Code text alone, fetched twice with distinct User-Agent strings and confirmed byte-identical.

expectedJSON.body: Taken together, the statutory provisions described in this document authorize four broad categories of benefit for a worker in a group the Department of Labor has certified as adversely affected by trade: (1) Trade Readjustment Allowances, which are weekly cash payments computed from the worker's own prior unemployment insurance benefit amount and payable only after the worker has exhausted regular unemployment insurance; (2) approved training, intended to help the worker qualify for suitable employment; (3) a job search allowance, reimbursing costs of looking for work outside the worker's local commuting area; (4) a relocation allowance, reimbursing moving costs and providing a lump-sum payment when a worker relocates for a new job; and, historically, (5) a health coverage tax credit toward the cost of health insurance premiums. This document does not state that Jordan Lee qualifies for any of these benefits, does not compute any amount Jordan Lee might receive, and is not a substitute for reviewing the current, effective text of 19 U.S.C. § 2271 et seq. and 26 U.S.C. § 35, including whatever transition or reauthorization provisions may apply after the termination date disclosed elsewhere in this document.

Jordan Lee acknowledges having received and reviewed this information sheet regarding the federal Trade Adjustment Assistance program, in connection with Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. that ended on March 2, 2026. This document is informational only. It does not itself constitute a TAA petition, application, or certification, and Jordan Lee understands that any such filing must be made directly with the U.S. Department of Labor and the applicable state agency.
